The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has announced the introduction of Video Assistant Referee (VAR) technology for all group-stage matches of the 2026/27 CAF Champions League and CAF Confederation Cup. The decision marks the first time VAR will be deployed throughout the group stages of both competitions, having previously been restricted to the knockout rounds. In a statement obtained from its website on Friday, CAF confirmed that the technology would be used in all group-stage fixtures, beginning with the 2026/27 Confederation Cup matches scheduled to kick off on Friday, November 27, 2026. Announcing the development, CAF said the introduction of VAR would provide additional support to match officials and contribute significantly to improving refereeing standards across the continent. The governing body stated that the move would help strengthen match officiating and ensure that African refereeing standards become “amongst the best in the world.” Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources The development is part of CAF’s broader efforts under its president, Dr Patrice Motsepe, to strengthen football infrastructure, invest in technology, develop referees and improve the professional organisation of its competitions. According to CAF, the implementation was made possible through its VAR Academy programme, which has provided the necessary technology and training for qualified Video Match Officials (VMOs) across all six CAF zonal unions. The organisation explained that specialised training courses at zonal and continental levels were helping to develop a larger pool of competent and experienced officials. It added that the expanded pool of trained officials would improve decision-making consistency and strengthen confidence in African refereeing. “This pool of highly qualified officials strengthen decision consistency, building trust in African refereeing and African Football,” the organisation stated. CAF has gradually expanded VAR deployment across its major competitions, including the Africa Cup of Nations, Women’s Africa Cup of Nations and the knockout stages of its interclub competitions. The latest decision represents another step in the continental body’s efforts to improve officiating, strengthen the credibility of its competitions and bring African football closer to international refereeing standards.
